sentences.sentence: Metoprolol is a beta-blocker medication used to treat high blood pressure, chest pain (angina), and heart failure, and to improve survival after a heart attack.
It works mainly on the heart, so it is called a cardioselective beta-blocker.
Metoprolol works by blocking the effect of adrenaline and noradrenaline on beta-1 receptors in your heart.
This slows your heart rate, reduces how hard your heart squeezes, and lowers your blood pressure.
Because the heart is doing less work, it needs less oxygen, which is why metoprolol also helps with angina.
Exactly how metoprolol works for high blood pressure, heart failure, and after a heart attack is not fully understood.
At higher blood levels, metoprolol also blocks beta-2 receptors in the airways and blood vessels, which is why it still needs care in people with breathing problems.
Metoprolol comes as two different salts, metoprolol tartrate and metoprolol succinate.
They are not interchangeable dose for dose:
Metoprolol tartrate , an immediate-release tablet usually taken once or twice a day (brand name Lopressor)
Metoprolol succinate , an extended-release tablet or capsule taken once a day (brand names Toprol-XL and Kapspargo Sprinkle)
Metoprolol tartrate is also given as an injection into a vein in a hospital during a heart attack.
The most common side effects of metoprolol are tiredness, dizziness, low mood (depression), diarrhea, shortness of breath, a slow heartbeat (bradycardia), and itching or rash.
Most side effects reported in studies were mild and did not last.
Get emergency medical help if you have signs of an allergic reaction to metoprolol: hives, difficulty breathing, or swelling of your face, lips, tongue, or throat.
In studies of people taking metoprolol for high blood pressure or angina:
Tiredness and dizziness occurred in about 10% of people
Low mood or depression was reported in about 5 out of 100 people
Diarrhea occurred in about 5% of people
Itching or rash occurred in about 5% of people
Shortness of breath and a slow heartbeat occurred in about 3% of people
Cold hands and feet, palpitations, swelling of the ankles, and low blood pressure were each reported in about 1% of people
Nausea, dry mouth, stomach pain, constipation, gas, and heartburn were each reported in about 1% of people
Headache, nightmares, trouble sleeping, confusion, and short-term memory loss have also been reported.

In the heart failure study of extended-release metoprolol, dizziness or vertigo was reported by 1.8% of people taking metoprolol compared with 1.0% taking placebo, and a slow heartbeat by 1.5% compared with 0.4%.
These have been reported since metoprolol came on the market.
Their frequency is not known:
Hair thinning or hair loss, which reversed after stopping
Reduced sex drive and difficulty getting an erection
Dry eyes, blurred vision, and ringing in the ears
Sweating, sensitivity to sunlight, and worsening of psoriasis
Change in taste, joint and muscle pain, and fainting
Liver inflammation (hepatitis)
A severe drop in white blood cells (agranulocytosis), which can show up as fever, chills, or a sore throat
Some of these, such as shortness of breath and a slow heartbeat, are also listed as common side effects above.
They need urgent attention when they are severe, new, or getting worse.
Call your doctor at once if you have:
A very slow heartbeat, pauses in your heartbeat, or a feeling that you might faint.
Sinus pause, heart block, and cardiac arrest have all been reported.
Signs that heart failure is getting worse, such as weight gain over a few days, more shortness of breath, or swelling of your feet or lower legs
Wheezing or trouble breathing
Chest pain that is worse or more frequent than usual, especially if you have recently stopped or missed doses
Cold, pale, or blue fingers and toes, or pain in your legs when you walk
Confusion, hallucinations, or memory problems
Yellowing of your skin or eyes, which can be a sign of liver inflammation
This is not a complete list of side effects and others may occur.
Call your doctor for medical advice about side effects.
You may report side effects to the FDA at 1-800-FDA-1088.
The most important warning with metoprolol is not to stop it suddenly.
Stopping a beta blocker abruptly can bring on worse chest pain and, in some cases, a heart attack.
If your treatment needs to stop, your prescriber will lower the dose gradually over 1 to 2 weeks and watch how you respond.
This applies even if you only take metoprolol for blood pressure, because heart disease is common and is not always known about.
Talk to your care team before starting metoprolol if any of these apply to you.
Asthma or other breathing problems.
Beta blockers can tighten the airways.
Metoprolol is used in people with these conditions only when other treatments are not suitable, at the lowest possible dose, with a reliever inhaler on hand.
Heart failure.
Heart failure can get worse while the dose is being increased.
Tell your doctor about weight gain or increasing breathlessness.
A slow heart rate or a conduction problem in the heart.
This includes first-degree heart block, sinus node problems, and Wolff-Parkinson-White syndrome.
Your heart rate should be monitored.
Diabetes or long gaps without food.
Metoprolol can hide the early warning signs of low blood sugar, such as a fast heartbeat, and can make low blood sugar more severe or last longer.
The risk is higher if you are fasting, not eating regularly, or vomiting.
An overactive thyroid.
Metoprolol can mask signs of an overactive thyroid.
Stopping it suddenly can trigger a thyroid crisis.
Circulation problems in your arms or legs.
Beta blockers can make symptoms of poor circulation worse.
A history of severe allergic reactions.
If you have anaphylaxis while taking a beta blocker, the usual dose of injectable epinephrine may not work as well.
Pheochromocytoma (a tumor of the adrenal gland).
Metoprolol must only be started after an alpha blocker has been started, or blood pressure can rise sharply.
Liver disease.
Metoprolol is broken down by the liver, so levels can build up.
Treatment is usually started at a lower dose.
Surgery.
Tell your surgeon and dentist that you take metoprolol.
Long-term beta blocker treatment is not usually stopped before surgery.

Starting a high dose of extended-release metoprolol shortly before non-cardiac surgery is avoided, because in one large trial this was linked to more slow heartbeats, low blood pressure, strokes, and deaths.

You should not take metoprolol if you have a very slow heart rate, heart block beyond the first degree, sick sinus syndrome without a pacemaker, cardiogenic shock, or heart failure that is not under control.
Metoprolol is not for you if you have:
Severe bradycardia (a very slow heart rate)
Second-degree or third-degree heart block, which is a fault in the heart's electrical signal
Sick sinus syndrome, unless you have a permanent pacemaker
Cardiogenic shock, when the heart cannot pump enough blood
Decompensated heart failure, meaning heart failure that is not stable
An allergy to metoprolol or to any of the other ingredients in your product
Immediate-release metoprolol tartrate tablets should also not be used if your top blood pressure reading is below 100 mmHg.
Take metoprolol at the same time each day, exactly as prescribed.
Do not change your dose or stop taking it without talking to your prescriber first.
Immediate-release metoprolol tartrate tablets should be taken with a meal or immediately after a meal.
For extended-release tablets and capsules, taking your dose with or just after a meal is preferred, but food does not have a significant effect on how much metoprolol your body absorbs.
Keep taking metoprolol even if you feel well.
High blood pressure often causes no symptoms.
Extended-release tablets are scored and can be split in half if your prescriber tells you to.
Swallow the whole or half tablet without crushing or chewing it.
Extended-release capsules (Kapspargo Sprinkle) should be swallowed whole.
If you cannot swallow the capsule, you can open it and sprinkle the contents over a teaspoon of soft food such as applesauce, pudding, or yogurt.
Swallow the mixture within 60 minutes and do not save any for later.
Tell your doctor if you are fasting or vomiting, because this raises your risk of low blood sugar.
Your blood pressure and heart rate will need checking regularly.
Store metoprolol at room temperature, between 68°F and 77°F (20°C to 25°C), away from moisture and heat.
Metoprolol injection is given into a vein by a healthcare professional in a coronary care unit or similar setting, where your blood pressure, heart rate, and heart tracing can be watched.
You are then switched to metoprolol tablets.
The usual starting dose is 25 mg to 100 mg once a day for extended-release metoprolol, and 100 mg a day for immediate-release metoprolol.
Your dose is then adjusted at intervals of a week or longer until your blood pressure or symptoms are controlled.

sentences.subsection_title: Metoprolol tartrate (immediate-release tablets) dosage for adults
sentences.sentence: With immediate-release tablets, a once-daily dose may not keep blood pressure controlled for the full 24 hours, especially at 100 mg. Splitting the dose or taking a larger daily dose may be needed.

sentences.subsection_title: Metoprolol succinate (extended-release tablets and capsules) dosage for adults
sentences.sentence: Kapspargo Sprinkle capsules are not suitable to start heart failure treatment if a dose below 25 mg is needed.
Extended-release metoprolol is the only form approved for children, and only for high blood pressure in children aged 6 years and older.
The starting dose is 1 mg for each kilogram of body weight once a day, up to a maximum first dose of 50 mg. Doses above 2 mg/kg, or above 200 mg a day, have not been studied.
Extended-release metoprolol has not been studied in children under 6 years.
Liver problems.
Start at a lower dose than usual and increase slowly.
Kidney problems.
No dose reduction is needed.
Older adults.
A low starting dose is generally used, because liver, kidney, and heart function are more often reduced and other medicines are more often involved.
Switching between forms.
When changing from immediate-release to extended-release metoprolol, the same total daily dose is used.

sentences.section_title: What happens if I miss a dose of metoprolol?
sentences.sentence: Skip the missed dose and take your next dose at the usual time.

sentences.section_title: What happens if I miss a dose of metoprolol?
sentences.sentence: Do not take two doses at once and do not double up to catch up.

sentences.section_title: What should I avoid while taking metoprolol?
sentences.sentence: Avoid driving and other tasks that need alertness until you know how metoprolol affects you.

sentences.section_title: What should I avoid while taking metoprolol?
sentences.sentence: It can make you feel tired or less alert.

sentences.section_title: What should I avoid while taking metoprolol?
sentences.sentence: Get up slowly from sitting or lying down, because metoprolol can make you feel dizzy or lightheaded.

sentences.section_title: What should I avoid while taking metoprolol?
sentences.sentence: Avoid alcohol if you take Kapspargo Sprinkle capsules.

sentences.section_title: What should I avoid while taking metoprolol?
sentences.sentence: Alcohol makes the capsule release its metoprolol much faster, which raises the risk of side effects.

sentences.section_title: What should I avoid while taking metoprolol?
sentences.sentence: Do not stop taking metoprolol on your own, even if you feel fine.
The interactions that matter most are medicines that also slow the heart and medicines that block the liver enzyme CYP2D6, which raises metoprolol levels in your blood.
Digoxin, clonidine, diltiazem, and verapamil.
These all slow the heart's electrical signal and heart rate.
Taking them with metoprolol raises the risk of a very slow heartbeat.
Clonidine, when stopping either medicine.
If you take both, the metoprolol is stopped several days before clonidine is slowly withdrawn, because beta blockers can worsen the blood pressure rebound that follows clonidine withdrawal.
Quinidine, fluoxetine, paroxetine, and propafenone.
These strong CYP2D6 blockers double the amount of metoprolol in your blood.
Quinidine tripled levels of one form of metoprolol and doubled how long it lasted.
Weaker CYP2D6 blockers are likely to raise levels too.
Reserpine and MAO inhibitors.
These deplete adrenaline-type chemicals and can add to metoprolol's effect, causing low blood pressure or a marked slowing of the heart.
Epinephrine.
If you need epinephrine for a severe allergic reaction, the usual dose may not work as well while you are on a beta blocker.
Other medicines that lower blood pressure or heart rate, including fingolimod, can add to metoprolol's effect.
Tell each of your healthcare providers about all medicines you take, including prescription and over-the-counter medicines, vitamins, and herbal products.
Not all possible interactions are listed here.

sentences.section_title: Can you take metoprolol during pregnancy or while breastfeeding?
sentences.sentence: Metoprolol crosses the placenta and passes into breast milk in small amounts.

sentences.section_title: Can you take metoprolol during pregnancy or while breastfeeding?
sentences.sentence: Tell your doctor if you are pregnant, planning a pregnancy, or breastfeeding.

sentences.section_title: Can you take metoprolol during pregnancy or while breastfeeding?
sentences.sentence: Studies published to date have not shown a link between metoprolol taken in pregnancy and major birth defects or miscarriage.

sentences.section_title: Can you take metoprolol during pregnancy or while breastfeeding?
sentences.sentence: Reports on growth restriction, early birth, and death around the time of birth have been inconsistent, and those studies have limitations that make them hard to interpret.

sentences.section_title: Can you take metoprolol during pregnancy or while breastfeeding?
sentences.sentence: Untreated high blood pressure and untreated heart failure in pregnancy carry their own serious risks for both mother and baby.

sentences.section_title: Can you take metoprolol during pregnancy or while breastfeeding?
sentences.sentence: Babies born to mothers taking metoprolol may have low blood pressure, low blood sugar, a slow heartbeat, or slow breathing, so they are watched after birth.

sentences.section_title: Can you take metoprolol during pregnancy or while breastfeeding?
sentences.sentence: The amount of metoprolol a breastfed baby receives is estimated at 0.05 mg to under 1 mg a day, which is about 0.5% to 2% of the mother's weight-adjusted dose.

sentences.section_title: Can you take metoprolol during pregnancy or while breastfeeding?
sentences.sentence: No side effects in breastfed babies have been identified.

sentences.section_title: Can you take metoprolol during pregnancy or while breastfeeding?
sentences.sentence: Babies are still monitored for a slow heartbeat and for signs such as unusual sleepiness.
